summary: Endianness is the order in which the bytes of a multi-byte value are stored in memory. Little-endian puts the least significant byte first; big-endian puts the most significant byte first. It matters whenever data crosses machines, files, or networks.

sections.heading: The two orders
sections.body: For the 32-bit value 0x12345678 stored starting at address 0:
sections.code:
address:        00 01 02 03
big-endian:     12 34 56 78   (MSB at lowest address)
little-endian:  78 56 34 12   (LSB at lowest address)

sections.heading: Who uses which
bullets: x86, x86-64, and most ARM systems run little-endian.
Network protocols use big-endian, called network byte order.
Some older architectures (SPARC, classic PowerPC, MIPS configurations) are big-endian; some CPUs are bi-endian.

sections.heading: Detecting host endianness
Network byte order functions
sections.body: Convert between host and network order with these functions from `<arpa/inet.h>`. They are no-ops on big-endian hosts and byte swaps on little-endian ones.
bullets: Use them for every multi-byte field you read from or write to a packet.
sections.code:
uint16_t port = htons(8080);
uint32_t addr = ntohl(pkt->src_ip);

sections.heading: Where it bites
bullets: Reading binary files written on another architecture.
Parsing protocol headers by casting a byte buffer to a struct.
Hash or checksum code that assumes a byte order.
Unicode UTF-16/32 text, which uses a Byte Order Mark (BOM) to declare order.

sections.body: Endianness describes byte order in memory. Bit numbering inside a byte is a separate convention (as in packet diagrams, where the most significant bit is drawn first). Protocol specs state both.

subtopics.title: Safe serialization
subtopics.summary: Never rely on struct layout for wire formats.

sections.body: Build packets by writing each field explicitly in a fixed order, or shift and mask: `buf[0] = v >> 8; buf[1] = v & 0xff;`. This is independent of host endianness, struct padding, and alignment.
sections.code:
static void put16(uint8_t *b, uint16_t v) { b[0] = v >> 8; b[1] = (uint8_t)v; }
static uint16_t get16(const uint8_t *b) { return (b[0] << 8) | b[1]; }

sections.body: GCC and Clang provide `__builtin_bswap16/32/64`, and Linux has `le32toh`, `be32toh`, and friends in `<endian.h>` for explicit conversions to and from a named order.

Big-endian reads naturally left to right and makes comparison of byte strings match numeric order. Little-endian lets a CPU read the low part of a value first and simplifies casting to a narrower type. Neither is faster in general; compatibility is the real cost.

takeaways: Endianness is byte order in memory: 0x12345678 is 12 34 56 78 (big) or 78 56 34 12 (little).
Network byte order is big-endian; use htons/htonl and ntohs/ntohl.
Serialize fields explicitly rather than casting buffers to structs.
Single bytes are unaffected; only multi-byte values care.
